newsitem.title: UK: Thatcher asks Blair not to fritter away her legacy.
newsitem.headline: Thatcher asks Blair not to fritter away her legacy.

text.p: Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher congratulated Britain's Labour leader Tony Blair on his election victory on Friday but warned him she would watch to ensure he did not fritter away the legacy of 18 years of Conservative rule.

Speaking to reporters outside her London home, Thatcher said Blair had skilfully concealed his detailed policies during the election campaign but had endorsed many of the principles that guided her and outgoing prime minister John Major over the past two decades.
"He fought an extremely skilful campaign. I don't know that we know very much about the policies. He has very carefully cloaked the details in soft words and phrases," Thatcher said.
Asked whether her legacy would be safe in the hands of Blair's new-look Labour Party, she said: "I shall have something to say if it is not."
Thatcher, who wore a dress in traditional Conservative blue, said it was unprecedented for a government to fight an election on such a strong economic record and go down to defeat.
"That is a strange factor. I don't think it has ever happened before that a government has done so well for its country -- we built it after a Labour disaster -- to be then turned out.
"Times change and you have to accept this result. So we will now start to rebuild the party for the future," she added.

Thatcher, who was forced out in an internal party coup in November 1990 after leading the Conservatives to three successive election victories, sidestepped questions about the party's looming leadership contest.

"That's not for me to decide. I have been through that once. I would never wish to go through it again," she said. Implicitly endorsing Major's swift decision to step down, Thatcher addded: "That's why I went to the (upper) House of Lords, so I could never be a rival."

Asked whether she felt more sorry for Major or for her erstwhile protege, former defence secretary Michael Portillo, who lost his North London seat, Thatcher said: "I'm sorry for all of those who lost. It's an experience I have never had."

John Major was the chosen heir of Britain's longest-serving premier of the 20th century but she constantly sniped at him from the sidelines, saying that he never seized the big ideas and "drifted with the tide".
